title: Replace a self-inking stamp's ink pad: lock the stamp down, swap the pad, unlock it
instruction: Replace the stamp's dry ink pad with the new one, put the dry pad in the tray, and leave the stamp standing ready to use.
context: Self-inking stamps (Trodat Printy, 2000 Plus, Colop) are used every day in offices, schools, post offices and shops, and their pad dries out and must be replaced. The makers' procedure (thestampmaker.com, Trodat self-inking stamps): "Push stamp down slightly and push buttons on side to lock into position. Pull out ink pad." 2000 Plus: "Push down slightly on the stamp - about 1/8 ... Lock the stamp in position using the locks on both sides of the stamp." The lock is released by pressing the stamp down again. At rest the spring holds the rubber text plate up in the pad's pocket, so a pad pulled without the lock catches and the light stamp just slides. One hand holds the body pressed 3 mm against its spring while the other squeezes the two small buttons at the stamp's ends; then a thin grip tab is pulled straight out, and the new pad is slid in level until its detent clicks.
setup: A table in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases: x forward, y to the robot's left. A self-inking stamp (Trodat Printy 4913 size: 7.4 x 3.8 cm footprint, 8.5 cm tall, 0.14 kg) stands upright, loose, at x 24, y 7, its length along x and its pad slot opening toward the robot's right (-y). In it, a dry ink pad (6.8 x 3.1 x 1.0 cm, 15 g, grey foam, white tab) with its grip tab (1.5 cm long, 1.8 cm tall, 2.5 mm thick) sticking out of the slot. A new pad (same, black foam, blue tab) lies ink side down on the desk at x 27, y -10, its tab toward -y. An open plastic tray (9 x 12 cm, 1.2 cm rims) is fixed at x 14, y -11. The stamp's lock buttons (1 x 0.8 cm) stand out 2.5 mm from its two ends, 6 cm up. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: Read every control step from the bodies' poses and the sliding parts' travel; finger distances from the fingers' collision meshes. Partial credit is the best stage reached, each needing the one before: 0.1 the stamp locked (body 2.0 mm or more down, both lock buttons pushed in 1.5 mm or more); 0.3 the dry pad out of the slot (its rear edge more than 1 mm in front of the frame's front face); 0.45 the dry pad in the tray (all of it inside the rims, lowest point within 15 mm of the floor), no finger within 1 cm of it; 0.6 the new pad fully home (rear edge within 1.0 mm of the back stop, where its detent clicks), case up within 15 deg (ink side down), dry pad still in the tray; 0.8 the stamp unlocked with the new pad home (both buttons out, less than 0.5 mm in; body back up, less than 0.5 mm down). 1.0: all of that at once, the stamp upright on its foot rails (within 10 deg), every finger 1 cm or more from the stamp and both pads, and everything still (moving less than 1 mm in 1 s). Doing nothing scores 0. On a real stamp the stages are judged from the videos and a final photo, and a test impression on paper confirms the new pad is home, ink side down, and the stamp unlocked.
reset_notes: Put the dry pad back in the stamp, fully home, unlock the stamp (body up), stand it at its mark, lay the new pad at its mark ink side down and empty the tray, as in the screenshot. In the simulation each trial starts the simulator afresh.
fidelity: Rigid bodies in Isaac Sim 6.1 (PhysX), 20 Hz control, at true size. The pad's soft foam is rigid: the text plate pressed into it is a rigid 1.5 mm boss in a 1.5 mm pocket, which traps the pad until the body is pressed 2.5 mm down. The body travels only 6 mm (no full stroke: the text plate never turns over to print). Springs are slide-joint drives; the detent is a sprung ball. No ink.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (both grippers hovered over the stamp and the new pad and nudged the stamp, but never pressed it down or pushed its lock buttons, so the dry pad stayed in); demo: 1.0
